text: I read supplied P as a finite-batch CVaR/obedience-cycle note and Q as a learning-augmented algorithms survey, so P\(\text{\textquoteright}s\) internal paper called Q is not our supplied Q. I will examine whether Q\(\text{\textquoteright}s\) cost/composition contract can turn P\(\text{\textquoteright}s\) expected empirical risk error into a realised, auditable downstream decision, or whether an impossibility/certification boundary is the sharper result.

I am testing a finite-batch conditional-CVaR oracle as an input to Q’s cost and composition framework. P already gives a cycle reversal and deterministic value-error certificates, so I will look for a distinct realised-batch, confidence-certified decision result with explicit sampling cost and a no-margin impossibility. I will keep Q’s survey-level claims separate from any new theorem.

Candidate certificate: assume each queried conditional loss is i.i.d. in \([0,U]\), upper-tail mass \(\beta>0\), and at most \(N\) action-signal cells are queried with \(m\) samples each. DKW plus the variational CVaR formula gives simultaneous realised errors \(e_m=(U/\beta)\sqrt{\log(2N/\delta)/(2m)}\) with probability \(1-\delta\). For a length-\(K\) cycle, its true sum lies within \(2Ke_m\) of its empirical sum. Declare feasible only when every relevant simple cycle lower bound is nonnegative; declare infeasible if one cycle upper bound is negative; otherwise abstain. This is a verifiable PAC decision, not unconditional exact feasibility. If each draw costs \(\kappa\), full sampling costs \(\kappa Nm\); Q’s per-invocation \(\kappa\) does not itself imply a per-draw cost.

Sharpened question: for P’s fixed one-type, finite-signal state-independent obedience test, can sampled conditional CVaR values produce a high-confidence exact yes/no certificate, with sampling charged explicitly? Q is a survey, not the mechanism paper named Q inside P: Q.tex lines 1035–1110 gives only conditional composition statements, and lines 1242–1258 defines a cost per predictor invocation. P.tex lines 24–43 already proves expected-empirical reversal; lines 49–72 already proves deterministic value-error cycle and common-reward tests, but explicitly excludes a realised-batch guarantee. New work must address realised samples and the cost conversion, not repackage these propositions.

Q is a survey, not the mechanism-design Q named inside P (P, §1 explicitly warns of this). Q §Pricing the Prediction (lines 1244–1258) defines a per-invocation charge \(\kappa\) and says exact \(1\)-consistency against an uncharged optimum fails with positive query cost; Q §Inference Graphs (1024–1109) requires conditional guarantees and benchmark/interface relations for composition. P Proposition 1 (lines 27–53) gives a reversal for every finite batch of expected empirical CVaR versus true CVaR; P Propositions 2–3 (lines 58–93) give a cycle-margin existence test and a rectangular-uncertainty common-reward graph test. These do not themselves certify one realised batch. Candidate sharpened question: with priced iid samples, can one output a state-independent reward plus a checkable high-probability certificate for true conditional-CVaR obedience, and what margin/cost is necessary?

No-margin obstruction is sharper than P’s expected-surrogate example. In P’s two-signal swapped-action construction take risky loss \(L=2X\), \(X\sim\mathrm{Bernoulli}(p)\), safe loss \(1\), tail mass \(\beta=1/2\), and prescribe risky at both signals. For \(p\in(0,1/2)\), true \(\mathrm{CVaR}_{1/2}(L)=4p\), so the two-edge cycle is \(C(p)=2-8p\): feasible at \(p_-=1/4-\varepsilon\), infeasible at \(p_+=1/4+\varepsilon\). Every finite binary transcript has positive probability under both, hence no zero-error finite-sample exact certificate can issue either answer. Any nonabstaining \(\delta\)-correct test for both has expected risky draws \(\mathbb E_{p_-}T\geq \operatorname{kl}(1-\delta,\delta)/\operatorname{kl}(p_-,p_+)\), thus sample cost diverges as \(\Omega(\kappa\varepsilon^{-2}\log(1/\delta))\) near the boundary. This is an explicit impossibility in the required decision model, not a general impossibility for all LAA or unrestricted rewards.

Priority caution: empirical-CVaR concentration and fixed-confidence best-CVaR-arm identification are already studied, including asymptotically optimal confidence intervals in a NeurIPS 2021 paper (https://proceedings.neurips.cc/paper/2021/file/d69c7ebb6a253532b266151eac6591af-Paper.pdf) and concentration plus fixed-budget identification in https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.00997. Search queries: “CVaR empirical concentration finite sample sample complexity risk constrained optimization certificate”; “sample based incentive compatibility verification cycle condition confidence intervals”; “CVaR empirical estimation lower bound sample complexity risk level”. Therefore DKW plus P’s existing graph test is a useful baseline, not by itself a credible novelty claim. A publication would need graph-aware adaptive priced sampling, a tight certificate complexity, or a substantive downstream composition theorem.

I wrote a full derivation in emmy/research.md. Beyond a yes/no test, P\(\text{\textquoteright}s\) rectangular graph yields a reward witness from the realised batch: with iid bounded conditional losses, \(N=|S||A|\), \(e_m=(U/\beta)\sqrt{\log(2N/\delta)/(2m)}\), use \(w_m(a,b)=\max_{s:a(s)=a}\{\widehat U(b,s)-\widehat U(a,s)+2e_m\}\). No positive graph cycle gives computable \(r(a)-r(b)\geq w_m(a,b)\), hence exact true obedience with probability at least \(1-\delta\). If every nontrivial true cycle has per-edge margin at least \(\gamma>0\), then \(e_m<\gamma/4\) suffices to certify; charging per draw gives \(\kappa_sNm\), whereas Q\(\text{\textquoteright}s\) per-invocation price needs a declared sample/invocation mapping. A failed graph test is abstention, not infeasibility. This supplies a witness-level result but no downstream competitive ratio absent Q\(\text{\textquoteright}s\) benchmark reduction.

Additional obstruction from Q’s observability point (Q.tex lines 975–980): P’s reward graph compares \(U(b,s)\) for deviating actions, so a realised-data certificate needs a generative conditional sampler, randomized exploration with coverage, or another identification model for every compared action-signal cell. On-policy logs alone may reveal only prescribed actions. In P’s swapped two-signal pattern, let each prescribed risky action have deterministic loss \(3/2\) in both worlds, while each unplayed safe deviation has loss \(2\) in world A and \(1\) in world B. On-policy observations are identical for arbitrarily many samples; the true cycle is \(+1\) in A and \(-1\) in B, so feasibility differs. This is a genuine no-identification result even with infinite logged data, separate from finite-sample margin complexity. It also limits the \(\kappa Nm\) bill: obtaining counterfactual samples must be feasible and priced.

Cost has two distinct meanings here. Q prices predictor invocations, but P\(\text{\textquoteright}s\) support theorem allows unrestricted action rewards; its no-positive-cycle condition does not bound the payment needed. For a true two-action cycle with edge requirements \(r(a)-r(b)\geq M\) and \(r(b)-r(a)\geq-M-\gamma\), \(\gamma>0\) makes exact support feasible, yet any nonnegative reward has cap at least \(M\). A costed downstream guarantee must declare a reward budget or payment objective as well as sample charge. With realised confidence weights \(w_m(a,b)\), adding \(0\leq r(a)\leq R\) to P\(\text{\textquoteright}s\) difference constraints gives a finite LP that certifies both exact obedience (on the coverage event) and a pathwise reward cap \(R\); Q\(\text{\textquoteright}s\) competitive ratio still needs a common benchmark.

Cross-check of Emmy’s #10: correct. The cycle criterion has no bound on reward magnitude. Two-edge requirements \(r(a)-r(b)\geq M\) and \(r(b)-r(a)\geq-M-\gamma\) have cycle weight \(-\gamma\leq0\), yet with \(r\geq0\) any feasible reward vector has \(\max_a r(a)\geq M\). Thus a “costed” certificate must separately declare whether rewards are real resource costs, impose a cap \(0\leq r(a)\leq R\), and solve P’s robust difference constraints with that cap. Sample acquisition cost \(\kappa Nm\) alone does not bound implementation expense. This is independent of Q’s need for a benchmark and failure-event cost control.

New costed refinement in emmy/research.md: with true graph edge \(w^*(a,b)=\max_{s:a(s)=a}[U(b,s)-U(a,s)]\), \(n=|A|\), and every simple cycle of distinct prescribed actions having average weight at most \(-\gamma<0\), the realised confidence graph satisfies \(w^*\leq w_m\leq w^*+4e_m\) simultaneously. If \(e_m<\gamma/4\), it has no positive cycle. Under nonnegative state-independent rewards, the coordinatewise minimal supporting reward is the maximum path-weight potential; simple paths have at most \(n-1\) edges. Thus minimum pathwise reward cap \(R_m^*\) for the sample-robust constraints obeys \(R^*\leq R_m^*\leq R^*+4(n-1)e_m\), where \(R^*\) is the true-utility oracle cap. With per-sample charge \(\kappa_s\), one decision has verifiable resource bound \(\kappa_sNm+R^*+4(n-1)e_m\) on the \(1-\delta\) coverage event. This is a local additive support-cost comparison, not a general competitive ratio. Proof and assumptions in emmy/research.md.

Priority/identification audit: empirical-CVaR concentration is prior work (https://arxiv.org/abs/1901.00997; https://arxiv.org/abs/1902.10709), and strict IC from a positive risk-value margin appears in a different persuasion model (https://arxiv.org/html/2605.12094v1, §5.3). The sequential KL lower-bound tool is standard (https://arxiv.org/abs/1407.4443). Ada\(\text{\textquoteright}s\) #9 counterfactual-data objection checks out: P\(\text{\textquoteright}s\) edges require losses for actions not taken at that signal; on-policy observations can be identical across feasible and infeasible worlds. Thus the baseline DKW-plus-graph result is a coherent bridge but weak publication novelty. The potentially stronger project is optimal cost-sensitive sampling and reward-cap certification under an explicit counterfactual access model, with matching bounds. Q\(\text{\textquoteright}s\) expected competitive-ratio framework additionally needs fallback/failure-event cost and benchmark control.

Cross-check of Emmy’s #12 support-cap refinement: it is correct under its declared positive cycle margin and nonnegative rewards. The interval event gives each true edge requirement \(w^*(a,b)\leq w_m(a,b)\leq w^*(a,b)+4e_m\). With no positive cycles, the coordinatewise minimal nonnegative reward is the maximum path-weight potential starting at each action; a maximal path can be simple, hence at most \(n-1\) edges. Therefore \(R^*\leq R_m^*\leq R^*+4(n-1)e_m\). This is a substantive local additive cost comparison, still conditional on counterfactual sample access and a confidence event; it is not Q’s competitive ratio. I will include it in ada/decision_certificate.md and retain the failure-cost and passive-log objections.

Best account now: sharpen the assigned question to a one-type, finite-signal, state-independent reward problem with upper-tail conditional CVaR and explicit counterfactual sampling. P\(\text{\textquoteright}s\) expected empirical risk can reverse exact feasibility; a realised-batch DKW box plus P\(\text{\textquoteright}s\) graph yields a checkable reward witness with probability \(1-\delta\), and nonnegative-reward path potentials give a local bill bound \(\kappa_sNm+R^*+4(n-1)e_m\) under strict cycle margin. Without margin, finite sample exact yes/no classification needs unbounded cost as the boundary is approached; without deviation samples, passive logs cannot identify feasibility at all. Exact expected system cost or competitive ratio remains unresolved without failure-event fallback, objective/benchmark relation, and reward-transfer accounting. The derivation and links are in emmy/research.md; this baseline alone is likely too incremental for publication given cited prior concentration and margin work.
ready at #15

Cost tuning from Emmy’s cap bound: under per-edge true cycle margin \(\gamma\), uniform batching needs \(m>m_{\min}:=8H^2\log(2N/\delta)/(\beta^2\gamma^2)\). The confidence-qualified sample-plus-one-payment upper bound is \(R^*+\kappa Nm+A m^{-1/2}\), where \(A=4(n-1)(H/\beta)\sqrt{\log(2N/\delta)/2}\). Its continuous minimizer subject to certification is \(m=\max\{m_{\min},(A/(2\kappa N))^{2/3}\}\), rounded upward with strict margin. This exposes a concrete price-versus-certification tradeoff; it is only an optimized sufficient upper bound, not an instance-optimal sampling result or Q competitive ratio.

Cross-checked Ada\(\text{\textquoteright}s\) #17: differentiating \(\kappa_sNm+A m^{-1/2}\) gives \(m_0=(A/(2\kappa_sN))^{2/3}\) for \(\kappa_s>0\), constrained by \(m>8U^2\log(2N/\delta)/(\beta^2\gamma^2)\). I added this to emmy/research.md. It is a valid optimization of the sufficient high-confidence sample-plus-reward-cap bound, not an optimal sample-complexity result. Remaining publication issue is a genuinely graph-aware adaptive allocation or tighter lower bound that accounts for reward expenditure and the counterfactual-data model.
ready at #18

Best account in ada/decision_certificate.md (style and artifact gates pass). Q.tex lines 257–265, 600–602, 1035–1109, 1242–1258 supply probability-space, fixed-decision-to-optimizer, composition, and per-invocation cost cautions; P.tex lines 24–43, 49–72, 92 supply expected-surrogate reversal, deterministic graph tests, and the realised-batch gap. Under bounded iid counterfactual conditional loss sampling, a simultaneous realised CVaR radius \(e_m=(H/\beta)\sqrt{\log(2N/\delta)/(2m)}\) gives a checkable graph reward witness or a negative-cycle witness, each sound with probability \(1-\delta\); otherwise abstain. With nonnegative rewards and per-edge cycle margin \(\gamma>4e_m\), path potentials yield a local sample-plus-one-payment bound \(\kappa Nm+R^*+4(n-1)e_m\), and a priced sufficient-batch optimum. Exact pathwise feasibility cannot be certified from finite samples uniformly near the boundary; expected draws scale at least \(\Omega(\gamma^{-2})\) for a nonabstaining high-confidence test. Passive on-policy logs alone cannot identify counterfactual deviation values even with infinite data. Publication judgment: the elementary bound is likely too incremental against existing CVaR identification and incentive-margin work; a defensible project is optimal graph-aware priced sampling with reward budgets and a proved downstream fallback/benchmark relation. Unresolved: counterfactual access model, tight instance-dependent complexity, failure-event cost, and whether transfers count as system cost.
ready at #20

Cross-check of Ada #20 against Q.tex lines 1035–1065: the displayed expected-cost bound \(\kappa Nm+B+\delta M\) needs the procedure to incur cost at most \(B\) on the whole confidence event, including any abstention branch; a bound only on accepted certificates is insufficient. A strict cycle-margin promise can force acceptance on that event, or a fallback cost can be included in \(B\). For Q-style adaptive composition, the sampling coverage statement must also hold conditionally on every reachable pre-sampling history (fresh conditional draws or an anytime-valid design), not merely marginally for one fixed policy. Neither condition follows from P.
ready at #22

I accepted Emmy #22 and amended ada/decision_certificate.md. The bound \(\mathbb E[\kappa Nm+D]\leq\kappa Nm+B+\delta M\) now assumes downstream cost \(D\leq B\) on the entire simultaneous-coverage event, including abstention, and \(D\leq M\) on every path. A strict cycle-margin promise can force certification on coverage; otherwise a specified fallback and its cost belong in \(B\). In a Q-style pipeline, coverage and cost bounds must hold conditionally on each reachable pre-sampling history (Q.tex lines 1035–1065), requiring fresh conditionally i.i.d. cell draws or an adaptivity-valid method. The note passes both artifact and style gates.
